title: Research session planning
scenario: A product researcher, designer, and operations partner plan adult usability sessions and leave recruitment and incentive questions open.
transcript:
[00:00] Tessa: Today I want to agree the tasks for the next usability round. We have a draft prototype and a list of questions, but those are not the same thing as a research plan. Let us start with what we actually need to learn before discussing how many people to invite.
[00:27] Malik: The main uncertainty is whether people can find the saved-items area after leaving the detail page. I moved the link in the prototype last week. It looks clearer to me, but that is an opinion from someone who knows the interface. I would like to observe the route people take.
[00:54] June: I also want to know whether the word collection makes sense. In the pilot conversation, one person thought it meant a paid subscription. That was one person's interpretation, so I would not treat it as a general finding yet. It does give us a useful question to explore.
[01:21] Tessa: Then we have navigation and terminology. I suggest a first task that asks someone to save two sample items, followed by an unrelated task, and then a request to find the saved items again. We should avoid saying collection in the task if that is the label we are testing.
[01:48] Malik: Agreed. If the facilitator names the tab, we would be measuring whether people can follow that hint. For the unrelated task, they could compare two delivery options in the prototype. Nothing should ask them to enter an address or make a purchase; all the information can stay fictional.
[02:15] June: The prototype currently has a blank address field that looks editable. Even if we tell people not to enter their own details, someone might assume that is necessary to continue. Can you replace it with a fixed sample location before we send the link to anyone?
[02:41] Malik: Yes, I can remove the editable field and use a fictional example by Wednesday afternoon. I will also check that the back button works on each path. A broken return path would make it hard to tell whether someone misunderstood the navigation or simply hit an unfinished screen.
[03:08] Tessa: Good. We will use fictional task data and no account creation. The plan should state that clearly. On terminology, I would prefer an open question after the navigation task: what would you expect to find here? That gives people room to describe their interpretation in their own words.
[03:35] June: That works. Please avoid asking whether the label is confusing. Some people will try to agree with the interviewer, especially after being told we are testing new wording. We can ask what they expected and whether the page matched that expectation without suggesting an answer.
[04:00] Malik: Should we show an alternative label in the same session? I have a version called saved items. If we show both, we could get a preference, but the second version will benefit from the participant already understanding the task. I am not sure that comparison would mean much.
[04:27] Tessa: Let us not compare labels within this round. We will observe the current version and collect interpretations. Choosing a replacement label is a later decision. If we need a comparison, we can design it properly rather than adding a preference question at the end of an already different session.
[04:54] June: For recruitment, the contact list has adults who previously opted into research invitations. We still need to check that the invitation scope covers this product area. I can verify that with the research coordinator tomorrow, but we should not send messages before that check is complete.
[05:20] Tessa: Please do that. We are not approving outreach today. Once you confirm the contact process, we can decide whom to invite. I had proposed six sessions in the draft, but that is a planning assumption, not a confirmed number. Availability may change what we can schedule.
[05:46] Malik: How long should the invitation say each session takes? I can do a demonstration of the whole prototype in fifteen minutes, but participants will need more time, and there should be space to explain the session and answer their questions before we begin the tasks.
[06:11] Tessa: Plan for thirty minutes, including the introduction and questions. The task sequence should fit within twenty so we do not rush the ending. We will tell participants they can pause or stop. We should not treat finishing every task as more important than respecting that choice.
[06:37] June: I can offer a written task list as well as reading the tasks aloud. That may help people who prefer to review the instructions themselves. We should use the same wording in both formats and present one task at a time so the later task does not reveal the navigation answer.
[07:05] Malik: I will make a simple task card layout. Does that mean we need a separate accessible version of the prototype? I can check keyboard operation, but I do not want to say it is fully accessible based on a quick pass that covers only these few screens.
[07:31] Tessa: Check keyboard operation for the planned paths and document any limitations. We should describe those limitations accurately when arranging a session. This research round does not certify the product's accessibility. If a path cannot be used, that is relevant evidence about the prototype, not a participant failure.
[07:57] June: There is an unresolved incentive question. The draft budget mentions a voucher, but I have not received confirmation of the amount or the purchasing process. I can ask operations tomorrow. Please leave the amount out of the invitation draft until we have an answer.
[08:22] Tessa: Agreed. No incentive amount is approved today. June will check the invitation process and incentive arrangements tomorrow. Malik has prototype fixes for Wednesday afternoon. I will write the facilitator guide and task wording by Thursday morning, using the scope we settled here.
[08:46] Malik: I can give you an earlier screenshot of the fixed sample location, but the complete path check will still be Wednesday afternoon. Please do not treat the screenshot as a ready prototype. I will explicitly mark the final handoff when the navigation checks are finished.
[09:11] June: I will draft the scheduling note after my checks, without sending it. It will offer thirty-minute appointments and mention that written instructions are available. We have not picked session dates, and I will leave those fields open until we know both participant and facilitator availability.
[09:36] Tessa: Before we close, the decisions are fictional task data, thirty-minute sessions, neutral task wording, and observation of one label in this round. Recruitment count, session dates, incentive amount, and a replacement label remain undecided. That is enough to move the preparation forward without pretending the study is already scheduled.
[10:03] Malik: That is clear. I will focus on making the agreed paths usable, not redesigning the whole prototype. If I discover a problem that changes the tasks, I will bring it back instead of quietly substituting a different test. Thanks; I have what I need.
